det_01.label: Epoch AI Notable AI Models — the source database
det_01.content: The data comes from Epoch AI's 'Notable AI Models' database, a curated catalogue of machine-learning models judged historically or technically significant. Epoch is a research institute that tracks the trajectory of AI by hand-collecting structured metadata (publication date, organization, domain, training compute, parameters, etc.) on each model. The full database spans from the 1950s to a 2026-05-18 snapshot and contains roughly 1,000 'notable' models in this extract (Epoch's broader AI-models database holds over two thousand entries). It is released under a Creative Commons Attribution license, free to reuse with credit. Crucially, this is a curated set, not a census of every model ever trained — which is exactly why it is useful for measuring the cadence of consequential releases rather than raw model spam.

det_02.label: What 'notable' means — the inclusion bar
det_02.content: A model qualifies as 'notable' in Epoch's database if it meets at least one of a small set of criteria: it advanced the state of the art on a recognized benchmark, was highly cited (on the order of 1,000+ citations), had significant real-world use (e.g. over a million monthly users), was historically important, or was expensive to train (on the order of $1M+). Models are typically added within about two weeks of release. This matters for interpretation: the curation bar is roughly constant over time, so a shrinking gap between notable releases reflects a real speed-up in consequential model output — not just a flood of trivial checkpoints. But the bar is also why point-releases and variants ('4.1', '4.5', 'Pro'/'Heavy') can each count as separate entries once they clear it.

det_03.label: The LLM race timeline that produced this acceleration
det_03.content: The cadence collapse is not an abstract statistic — it tracks a well-documented arms race. The Transformer arrived in 2017; GPT-2 (2019) and GPT-3 (2020, 175B parameters) established large language models as a category. The inflection point was ChatGPT in November 2022, which reached 100 million users in two months — the fastest-growing consumer app in history at the time. That triggered Google's internal 'code red', Microsoft's $10B investment in OpenAI, Meta's decision to open-source Llama, and a surge of capital into Anthropic. GPT-4 followed in March 2023. From there a stable cast of frontier labs — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google/Google DeepMind, Meta AI, xAI, DeepSeek, Mistral AI, Alibaba — began shipping flagship and point releases on ever-tighter schedules. The dataset's 2022-onward gap collapse is the quantitative fingerprint of exactly this competitive escalation.

det_04.label: Independent confirmation: the pace is breaking eval cycles
det_04.content: External trackers corroborate the acceleration and add a 'so what'. Industry coverage in 2026 notes that frontier labs are 'releasing new models faster than ever', with the three leading labs now updating flagship models 'every few weeks, not every few months' — to the point that the pace itself is becoming a barrier to entry for smaller competitors. A Frontier Model Release Velocity Index reported roughly 12+ substantive frontier releases in Q1 2026 versus 6 in Q4 2025, a sustained pace near three meaningful launches per week. The downstream consequence: organizations that historically ran six-month model-evaluation cycles are being forced onto roughly four-week cadences, because the top model on a router like OpenRouter can change two or three times within a single quarter. This is the real-world stake behind the median-gap numbers.

det_05.label: Caveat: a 'release' in 2025 is a smaller increment than in 2019
det_05.content: The headline 30x speed-up is real but must be read carefully. Part of the cadence collapse comes from more labs entering the race and from point-releases and variants ('4.1', '4.5', 'Pro', 'Heavy', 'Thinking' editions) each clearing the notability bar as separate entries. That is itself part of the iteration-speed phenomenon being measured — labs ship smaller, more frequent increments — but it means a single 'release' today represents a smaller capability jump than a flagship release in 2019. The median-gap metric is robust to the partial 2026 year (data runs through mid-May, so 2026's annual COUNT is incomplete, but its gap of ~4 days is unaffected). Pre-2017 years have tiny sample sizes and noisy gap values that should be ignored; the clean trend runs 2019 to present.

det_06.label: Scope suggestion for the Analyst
det_06.content: The cleanest story lives in two derived tables. (1) frontier_cadence_by_year.csv: the field-wide median days between consecutive Language-domain frontier releases, bucketed by year — this is the headline metric and is the most defensible because the median is robust to the partial 2026 year and to outliers. (2) frontier_release_gaps.csv: within-lab release-to-release gaps for each of the named frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google/Google DeepMind/DeepMind, Meta AI, xAI, DeepSeek, Mistral AI, Alibaba), which lets you show that individual labs follow the same pattern, not just the pooled field. models_per_year.csv (annual notable-model volume) supports the macro 'more models overall' backdrop but its 2026 value is partial and must be flagged. Focus the analysis on 2018->2026 for cadence and treat pre-2017 gaps as noise.

reference_media.description: No reference media collected. This is an abstract, quantitative time-series dataset about AI release cadence. Real-world photos (lab logos, product screenshots) would be generic, brand-encumbered, and add no evidentiary value. The story is best told with data-driven charts plus at most one atmospheric hero image generated by the Designer. Omission is intentional, not an oversight.
